R0.p: A person is held prisoner or in captivity.

R1.r: *Dickson 116 n. 44, 122; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 319 n. 152.
R1.p: A wild man is caught and then made tame and domesticated.

R2.p: God keeps the devil locked up as a prisoner for three years.

R3.p: A king locks up the envoy or ambassador sent to him by another king.

R4.p: An enemy or victim is caught by surprise and taken prisoner.

R4.1.p: An enemy is caught unawares while bathing and is taken captive.

R5.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
R5.p: A person is taken prisoner on the battlefield during fighting.

R5.1.p: An enemy army is trapped inside walls of earth thrown up by the hero's chariot wheels.

R5.2.p: A hero is captured when enemies press in on him from all sides with their shields.

R6.p: Death, personified as a messenger or figure, is locked up so that people stop dying.

R7.p: Men are kept as prisoners in a land ruled by women.

R8.p: Gods are taken prisoner by a mortal or another power.

R9.p: Miscellaneous tales in which someone or something is held captive and no other category fits.

R9.1.p: The sun is captured and held prisoner.

R9.1.1.p: The sun is caught while visiting the earth and is held there.

R9.1.2.p: The sun and moon are seized by a creditor, which causes an eclipse.

R9.1.3.p: The sun and moon each hold the other prisoner.

R9.2.p: Grain and pulse, in human form, are imprisoned by a wicked king.

R9.3.p: An ogress is captured and then reformed.

R9.4.p: A fire-maiden is shut up in an iron house.

R9.5.p: A cow is kept imprisoned until it promises not to eat men.

R9.6.p: A king imprisons all living creatures.

R10.r: **Feilberg Bjærgtagen (København, 1910), Nissens Historie; **Hdwb. d. Märchens I 541ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 86, (Zuñi): Benedict II 334.
R10.p: A general motif of a person being carried off by force and held against their will.

R10.1.r: (Cf. R11.1, R12.1, R13.1, R16.1, R17.1, R25.1, R31.) *Types 301, 302, 311, 312; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 553b nn. 296—315; Feilberg Bjærgtagen (København 1910).—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “princesse”; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 133—135; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Grote I 156; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 220.
R10.1.p: A princess or young woman is seized and carried away against her will.

R10.1.1.p: A young woman is seized and carried off by a band of soldiers.

R10.1.2.p: A young man secretly takes a girl away from her harsh father and brother, usually with her consent.

R10.2.p: A person stages their own kidnapping to hide an affair or cover a plan. In the noted case, an unfaithful wife arranges to be carried off by her lover.

R10.3.p: Children are taken away by force.

R10.4.p: A witch carries off a hero because she is in love with him.

R10.4.1.p: A giantess plans to abduct the bridegroom and kill the bride as revenge.

R11.r: (Cf. G440.) **Feilberg Bjærgtagen (København, 1910); Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 133—135, III Nos. 141f.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 129, 1060; S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 39.
R11.p: A person is carried off by a monster, such as an ogre.

R11.1.r: (Cf. R10.1.) *Types 301, 302, 311, 312; *BP I 398, 404, II 301, 317, III 434; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 544b, 547a nn. 60—79, 140—174; *Fb “brud” IV 64b.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Korean: Zong in-Sob 221 No. 98; Japanese: Dixon 215 n. 17; Eskimo (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 167; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 341f. nn. 228, 228a, 231, 235.
R11.1.p: A princess or young woman is carried off by a monster or ogre.

R11.1.1.p: A girl is carried off by a half-animal man who has hair all over his body and dog's claws.

R11.2.p: A person is carried off by the devil.

R11.2.1.r: Scala Celi 6b, 43a, 54b, 77b Nos. 39, 246, 306, 441; Fb “fanden” I 267a; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 55, Beal XXI 322; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 13 Nos. 116, 118; Spanish Exempla: Keller; West Indies: Flowers 571.
R11.2.1.p: The devil carries away wicked people.

R11.2.1.1.p: The devil carries off an emperor as punishment for the many people he has murdered.

R11.2.2.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 507, 1053; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 3/1386).
R11.2.2.p: A person is carried off by a demon.

R11.2.2.1.p: A person is carried off by the personified Echo.

R11.3.r: (Cf. F531, G100.) English romance: Malory V 5; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 166 No. 72; N. A. Indian (Zuñi): Benedict II 334.
R11.3.p: A person is carried off by a giant.

R12.p: A person is carried off by pirates.

R12.1.r: (Cf. R10.1.) *Reinhard PMLA XXXVIII 465; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 981.
R12.1.p: A young woman is seized and carried away by pirates or robbers.

R12.2.r: French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
R12.2.p: A man is seized and carried away by pirates.

R12.2.1.p: A child is kidnapped by robbers and raised to follow their criminal ways. The man later becomes wealthy and law-abiding.

R12.3.p: A pair of lovers is seized and carried off by pirates.

R12.4.p: A girl is lured into a boat and then kidnapped.

R13.p: A person is carried off by an animal, which takes the captive away from home.

R13.0.1.p: Children are carried away by animals.

R13.1.p: A person is abducted by a wild beast.

R13.1.2.p: A lion carries off a child.

R13.1.3.p: A rhinoceros carries off a man.

R13.1.4.p: A person is abducted by a tiger.

R13.1.4.1.p: A tiger carries off a man.

R13.1.4.2.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 142.
R13.1.4.2.p: A tiger carries off a woman.

R13.1.4.2.1.p: Tigers carry off a princess to become the wife of their human ward.

R13.1.5.p: A wolf carries off a person.

R13.1.6.p: A bear carries off a girl and makes her his wife.

R13.1.11.p: A fox carries a person off, taking them captive as a wild beast would.

R13.2.p: A person is carried off by a tame or domestic animal.

R13.2.1.p: A ram carries off a girl.

R13.2.2.p: A bull carries off the devil after the devil has tried to trick God.

R13.2.3.p: A cat carries a person off.

R13.2.3.1.p: A goddess's cat carries a person off.

R13.3.r: German: Grimm No. 51; India: *Thompson-Balys; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 183, 201; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 79; Africa (Yoruba): Frobenius Atlantis X 222ff. No. 14.
R13.3.p: A bird carries a person off.

R13.3.2.p: An eagle carries a young man away.

R13.4.p: A reptile carries a person off.

R13.4.1.p: A snake carries a person off.

R14.r: Greek: Grote I 35, 83, 261; India: *Thompson-Balys; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 183.
R14.p: A god or demigod carries a person off.

R16.p: A person who has taken another shape carries someone off.

R16.1.r: (Cf. D658, D2121.7, R10.1.) *Type 516; Rösch FFC LXXVII 112; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 57 No. 425.
R16.1.p: A hero in transformed shape carries off a maiden.

R16.2.p: A werewolf carries off a child.

R16.3.p: A fairy in transformed shape carries off a woman.

R16.4.p: A man who has become a tiger carries someone off.

R16.5.p: A man who has become an elephant carries someone off.

R17.r: (Cf. D1520.28.) Hartland Science 175; Icelandic: Boberg; Japanese: Ikeda; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 160 No. 23.
R17.p: A whirlwind carries a person away.

R17.1.p: A whirlwind carries a princess away.

R18.p: A woman or man is carried off by a suitor whose advances they had earlier rejected, taking revenge through abduction.

R22.p: A captive is carried off after being drugged with a sleep-inducing potion or drink.

R22.1.p: The victim is given a sleeping drug and then wrapped up in a cloak to be carried off.

R22.2.p: The victim is lulled into a deep sleep by music and then abducted.

R23.p: A captive is carried off by an abductor who uses a magic mask that makes the abductor invisible.

R24.p: The abductor carries off the captive while disguised as someone else.

R24.1.p: A prince takes the princess away by pretending to be a holy man.

R24.2.p: A prince who wants a princess disguises himself as a minstrel and carries her away.

R25.p: The captive is carried off through a secret tunnel running underground.

R25.1.r: (Cf. R10.1.) *Type 516; Rösch FFC LXXVII 102; BP I 46ff.; Icelandic: Boberg.
R25.1.p: A princess is taken away through a secret underground tunnel.

R31.r: (Cf. R10.1.) Icelandic: *Boberg; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 343 n. 237.
R31.p: The lights are put out so that a woman can be stolen away in the dark.

R32.p: Someone steals the clothes of people bathing, so that they cannot leave and can be carried off.

R33.p: A fairy healer is taken away by force to cure mortals who have been wounded.

R35.p: A princess who has been abducted gives birth to a child while in captivity.

R39.p: A miscellaneous abduction that does not fit the more specific categories in this section.

R39.1.p: A captive is carried off by a magician.

R39.2.p: A captive is carried off by an old woman.

R40.p: Describes the kinds of places where captives are kept imprisoned.

R41.p: A captive is kept imprisoned in a tower, castle, or prison.

R41.1.r: *Type 400; English: Wells 66 (Ywain and Gawain); Irish myth: *Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys.
R41.1.p: A captive is kept imprisoned in a castle.

R41.1.1.p: A captive is held inside a palace that lies underground.

R41.2.r: *Type 310; Dickson 198 n. 8; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 1, IV No. 6, Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
R41.2.p: A captive is held prisoner in a tower, castle, or similar prison.

R41.2.1.p: A wife falsely accused of slander is shut in a tower for forty days; if no champion comes forward to defend her she is to be burned, but a former suitor rescues her.

R41.2.2.p: A captive is kept confined in a bower, a shady leafy retreat or private chamber.

R41.3.r: Irish myth: *Cross; English: Wells 22 (Sir Beues of Hamtoun); Jewish: Neuman.
R41.3.p: A captive is held in a dungeon, a dark underground prison cell.

R41.3.1.r: (Cf. Q465.1.) *Boje 92; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 436b nn. 183—198; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
R41.3.1.p: A captive is imprisoned in a dungeon filled with snakes.

R41.3.2.p: A captive is imprisoned in a dungeon that has a stream of water running through it.

R41.3.3.p: A captive is imprisoned in a dungeon whose floor is covered with spikes, so that standing or lying there is painful or deadly.

R41.3.4.p: A captive is imprisoned by being kept down in a well.

R41.4.p: A bridegroom is held prisoner in the bridal chamber he shares with a giantess.

R41.5.p: An abducted princess is chained in a hall with one hundred doors, and a bridal bed is prepared for her and the giant in the middle of it.

R41.5.1.p: A captive queen is kept in a palace of forty doors, each guarded by a dog.

R41.6.p: A captive is imprisoned inside a pillar.

R41.7.p: A captive is kept confined in cages.

R42.p: A captive is held in a sunken valley, a hollow place below the surrounding land.

R43.p: A captive is held prisoner on an island.

R45.r: *Type 870; *BP III 443ff., 450; *Fb “höj” I 740b, 741; **Liungman Traditionsstudie över sagan om prinsessan i jordkulan (Göteborg, 1925). — Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 54 No. 405*A; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
R45.p: A captive is held in a mound, cave, or hollow hill, such as a fairy hill.

R45.1.r: N. A. Indian (Seneca): CurtinHewitt RBAE XXXII 705 No. 135.
R45.1.p: A man is buried alive, confined under the roots of a tree.

R45.2.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 5; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman.
R45.2.p: A captive is thrown into a lion's den to be held there.

R45.3.p: A captive is kept confined in a cave.

R45.3.1.p: A bear keeps a human wife captive in a cave, sealing the entrance with a stone.

R46.p: A captive is held prisoner under water, in the sea, a lake, or a river.

R47.p: A captive is held prisoner in the lower world, the underworld or realm of the dead.

R49.p: A captive is held in some other place of imprisonment not covered by the more specific headings.

R49.1.p: A captive is held prisoner inside a tree.

R49.2.p: A captive is shut up in an oven.

R49.3.p: An ogre seizes a girl and shuts her up inside a drum.

R50.p: Describes the conditions or treatment under which captives are kept.

R51.p: Captives are treated cruelly or abused while they are held prisoner.

R51.1.p: Prisoners are deliberately left to starve.

R51.2.p: Prisoners are kept bound in chains.

R51.3.p: Prisoners have their bodies mutilated or maimed.

R51.4.p: A prisoner is killed in a massacre.

R53.p: Captivity serves as a hiding place or protection, so that the person held is kept safe from others.

R53.1.p: A woman hides in an underground chamber or in a mud hut to stay safe.

R53.2.p: A woman is hidden in a sacred place that her lover is not supposed to dare to enter.

R53.3.p: A girl is locked up to delay her wedding.

R53.4.p: A faithful servant locks his master and the master's friend in a small house built from wood salvaged from their wrecked ships; the two men wrongly believe they have been betrayed.

R54.p: A hero is locked up while his father is murdered.

R61.r: *Types 506, 888; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; Africa (Fang): Einstein 151.
R61.p: A person is sold into slavery.

R70.p: Describes how captives behave while they are held prisoner.

R71.p: A captive prince, freed by the man who held him, becomes that man's companion out of gratitude for his freedom.

R72.r: (Cf. M165.) Hdwb. d. Märchens II “Gnade ausbitten”; Icelandic: Boberg.
R72.p: Defiant imprisoned men refuse their father's pardon unless it is offered to all of them together.

R74.p: Defeated warriors join the conqueror and serve in his army or household.

R74.1.p: A defeated enemy becomes the conqueror's closest friend.

R74.2.p: The son of a defeated enemy becomes the conqueror's loyal man.

R74.3.p: A defeated enemy keeps his rank and his land if he promises to pay tribute to the conqueror.

R74.3.1.p: A captive king's son is set free when he promises to be a faithful subject and pay tax to his captor.

R75.p: A person or group gives up to an enemy and stops resisting.

R75.1.p: Defeated people hand their city over to the conqueror.

R75.2.p: Warriors give up fighting and surrender after their chief dies.

R75.2.1.p: Warriors run away after their chief dies.

R81.r: **Köhler-Bolte I 373, II 387; *Fb “datter” IV 94b; *DeCock Studien en Essays 23ff.; *Crane Vitry 232f. No. 238; *Oesterley No. 215; Herbert III 220; Alphabet No. 166; Scala Celi 39a No. 220; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 28.—Spanish: Keller, Espinosa II No. 17; Jewish: Neuman.
R81.p: A woman nurses an imprisoned relative by passing her milk to him through the prison wall.

R81.1.p: A woman nurses her husband who is stranded on a rock.

R82.p: A captive secretly sends a message outside, hidden in an orange or on a handkerchief.

R83.p: A baker disguises himself as an old woman and takes the princess's place in her cell when he brings her bread.

R84.p: A prisoner is kept alive by food that is supplied from outside the prison.

R85.p: An angel protects a captive from the person who abducted him.

R100.p: A heading for tales in which captives or people in danger are freed.

R110.p: A captive is freed from confinement or danger by someone who rescues him.

R110.1.p: A goddess frees a man thrown into jail and returns his goods to him.

R111.r: (Cf. H1385.1, R10.1.) *Sparnaay 45ff.; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 550a nn. 219, 220, 554b; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “princesse”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 18; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 133—35, III Nos. 140, 143; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 334ff.
R111.p: A captive young woman is freed from the people or place holding her.

R111.0.1.p: A rescuer who brings back a stolen daughter is promised all of the father's property.

R111.1.p: A princess or maiden is rescued from the one who has captured her.

R111.1.1.r: See references to R11.1. Type 590; BP III 1; *Basset RTP III 562; English: Wells 64 (The Avowynge of King Arthur), 66 (Ywain and Gawain), 70 (Libeaus Disconus); Irish myth: *Cross: Spanish: Espinosa III No. 143; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 3; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 307, 359; N. A. Indian (Zuñi): Benedict II 341.
R111.1.1.p: A princess is rescued from an ogre who holds her.

R111.1.2.r: *Types 506B, 970**; *BP III 490ff.; *Liljeblad Tobiasgeschichte; Icelandic: Boberg; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 7; India: *Thompson-Balys.
R111.1.2.p: A princess is rescued from a band of robbers.

R111.1.3.r: *Types 300, 303; *Hartland Perseus III 1—65 passim; **Ranke FFC CXIV; *BP I 534; *Loomis White Magic 119. See also references to B11.10 and B11.11. — Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos. 133—135, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 68f.; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 158 n. 3; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
R111.1.3.p: A princess or maiden is rescued from a dragon.

R111.1.4.r: (Cf. G100.) *Dickson 132 n. 106; *Brown Iwain 50 n. 1; Irish myth: *Cross; English: Wells 117 (Sir Torrent of Portyngale); Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
R111.1.4.p: A princess or maiden is rescued from a giant or other monster.

R111.1.5.p: A woman is rescued from her husband, who is a snake.

R111.1.6.p: A princess is ransomed or bought back from slavery.

R111.1.6.1.p: A queen is rescued or ransomed from slavery.

R111.1.7.p: A princess is rescued from a magician who holds her.

R111.1.8.p: Several maidens are rescued from witches.

R111.1.9.p: A princess is rescued from a suitor she does not want.

R111.1.10.p: A princess or queen, won by a supernatural being in a game of chance, is rescued from him.

R111.1.11.p: A maiden is rescued from a rakshasa, a demon in Indian lore.

R111.1.12.p: A princess is rescued from being held captive by an elephant.

R111.1.13.p: A girl is rescued from tigers that hold her.

R111.1.13.1.p: A woman is rescued from a bear's cave where she is held.

R111.2.p: A princess is rescued from the place where she is held captive.

R111.2.1.r: *Type 301; *BP II 300; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 25; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa II 133—135; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Dixon 215.
R111.2.1.p: One or more princesses are rescued from the underworld or lower world.

R111.2.1.1.p: A woman who has been stolen is rescued from the underworld, the realm below the earth where she was taken.

R111.2.2.r: *Type 530; *BP III 111; Icelandic: De la Saussaye 143, 144 (Siegfried and Brunhilde).
R111.2.2.p: A princess is rescued from a mountain where she has been held captive.

R111.2.3.p: A princess is rescued from a giant's cave, where she is tied by her hair to a chair.

R111.2.3.1.p: An earl's daughter is rescued from a giant's cave where she is chained to a pillar or wall.

R111.2.4.r: Icelandic: Bósa saga 30ff ch. 8, 114ff ch. 12, Boberg.
R111.2.4.p: A princess is rescued from a temple where she is kept imprisoned.

R111.2.5.p: A girl is rescued from a tree where she has been held or left.

R111.3.p: The ways or methods by which a captive princess is rescued.

R111.3.1.p: A girl is rescued by being carried away through the air, for example by flying.

R111.4.p: A hero rescues a princess and returns her to the man she is promised to marry.

R111.5.p: A nobleman rescues a noblewoman from a servant who had betrayed her.

R111.6.p: A girl is rescued and then left behind or deserted by her rescuer.

R111.7.r: Type 653; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Konde): Gemuseus und Berger ZsES XXIII 1ff., (Tanga): Nassau JAFL XXVIII 30ff. No. 5, (Vai): Ellis 200f. No. 18.
R111.7.p: Two rescuers who saved a princess quarrel over who gets her.

R111.8.p: A person who has been rescued is taken away again from the rescuer.

R111.8.1.p: A rescued woman is stolen away from her rescuer by a demon.

R111.8.2.p: A rescued woman is stolen away from her rescuer by other men.

R112.r: (Cf. R45.) *Fb “höj” I 740b; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Espinosa III No. 140; India: Thompson-Balys.
R112.p: A prisoner is freed from a mound or hill by magic.

R112.1.p: Before sunrise, three blasts on a horn are sounded to free a prisoner from a mound.

R112.2.p: A rescuer rides three times around a hill to free a captive shut inside it.

R112.3.p: Prisoners are rescued from a fairy stronghold.

R115.p: A king who has been changed into a parrot frees captive parrots.

R115.1.p: A husband is turned into a mouse so he can slip into the cave prison where his wife is held.

R116.r: (Cf. R111.1.2.) *Type 851; BP I 188ff.; French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
R116.p: A captive is rescued from a den of robbers.

R117.p: Someone is saved from being burned to death.

R121.p: Various ways a captive is freed from prison.

R121.1.r: Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 280 No. 91, 283 No. 92.
R121.1.p: A princess is pulled up through a prison window by hand and so set free.

R121.2.p: The rescuer pretends to be the captive and fools a blind guard, so the real captive slips away.

R121.3.p: A house is burned or torn down to free a man who is trapped inside it.

R121.4.p: Ants carry silk threads to a prisoner, who uses them to make a rope and escape.

R121.5.r: *Herbert III 204; Oesterley No. 63; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 135 n. 3.
R121.5.p: A prisoner is given a thread to follow so he can find his way out of a labyrinth where he is held.

R121.6.r: (Cf. R165.) Alphabet No. 436; *Loomis White Magic 89, 93; Icelandic: *Boberg.
R121.6.p: A saint enters the prison and breaks the chains, freeing the prisoner.

R121.6.1.p: A saint appears in a vision to the prisoner's captor and orders that the prisoner be released.

R121.6.2.p: Locks open by themselves for a particular person, letting them out of confinement.

R121.7.p: Lovers are freed from prison by paying a ransom.

R121.8.p: A fairy mound is destroyed so that a person held inside it can be rescued.

R121.9.p: A stream carries messages between a prisoner and the person trying to rescue him.

R121.10.p: A woman uses her teeth to file through the chain that ties up her husband.

R122.p: A captive is rescued by some miraculous, supernatural means.

R122.1.p: A prisoner is whisked away in a blaze of fire.

R122.2.p: A prisoner is carried off by a cloud.

R123.p: After someone prays, a widow's son is granted a favor and is released from prison.

R130.p: Various rescues of people who have been abandoned or lost.

R131.r: Gaster Oldest Stories 171; Icelandic: *Boberg; Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 19, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 138—41; India: *Thompson-Balys.
R131.p: A baby who has been left out to die is found and saved.

R131.0.1.p: A nurse goes from door to door begging for food so she can keep the child she has been entrusted with and raise him.

R131.0.2.p: Every child who has been exposed or abandoned is saved by a miracle.

R131.1.r: *Type 930; *Aarne FFC XXIII 56, 59; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Fox 22 (Telephos), 57 (Atalanta).
R131.1.p: A hunter finds an abandoned child and rescues him.

R131.2.r: *Types 707, 930; BP II 380ff.; *Aarne FFC XXIII 61; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 116.
R131.2.p: A miller finds an abandoned child and rescues him.

R243.1.p: A helpful animal misdirects the pursuer so that the fugitive can get away.

R244.p: Ships are burned so that the people cannot flee by sea.

R245.r: As a consequence the whale runs into the shore or is killed by lightning.) *Loomis White Magic 91; cf. Aarne FFC XXIII 137; Maori: Dixon 8; N. A. R245.p: A man is carried across water on the back of a whale, which is a kind of fish.

R245.1.p: A trickster props a crocodile's jaws open and then leaves it, so the crocodile serves as a boat to carry him across water.

R245.2.p: A snake king carries fleeing captives across a river.

R246.p: Fugitives on the run are carried across a stream by a crane who lets them cross along his leg. The pursuer is either refused help by the crane or is drowned by it.

R246.1.p: A stone bridge suddenly appears to help fugitives cross, and when pursuers try to follow it vanishes so they drown.

Cf. Thompson Tales 341 n. 230. Most African references in B421.
R251.p: Fugitives escape by climbing into a tree, and an ogre tries to chop the tree down to reach them.

R252.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 92.
R252.p: Fugitives flee by vaulting ahead with the help of a magic stick.

R253.p: A captive escapes from a giant bird's nest by grabbing two of its young birds and leaping away with them.

R255.r: “Behind me night and before me day that no one shall see where I go.” *Type 510B; *BP II 46; Ainu: Ikeda (Type 175).
R255.p: A fixed formula is recited by a fleeing girl, naming the things behind and ahead of her, such as the night behind her.

R257.p: Fugitives keep themselves alive on a diet of apples during their flight.

R260.p: Pursuit scenes in which one party chases another, usually fugitives trying to get away.

R261.p: A pursuer is chasing the fugitive by sending a rolling object after them.

R261.1.r: *Kittredge Gawain and the Green Knight 189 n. 1; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 343 nn. 238, 238a, *Alexander N. A. Myth. 290 n. 37; cf. R261.1.p: A pursuer chases the fugitive by rolling a severed head after them.

R262.p: A magic eel chases a man across land in pursuit.

R265.r: Fb “hale” IV 197b; cf. Burns “Tam O’ Shanter”; India: Thompson-Balys.
R265.p: A pursuer such as a witch or giant catches the fugitive's horse by pulling out its tail, slowing the escape.

R267.p: Fugitives drop mustard seeds or ashes from a bag, which then mark their trail so pursuers can follow.

R268.p: Dew on the grass shows the pursuers the footprints of a fugitive, revealing which way he went.

R271.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 82.
R271.p: Fugitives are pursued by fire, which chases them and threatens to catch them.

R272.p: A pursuer follows the fugitives from one night's campfire to the next, each fire brighter than the last.

R300.p: Fugitives and captives find refuge in hiding places, and are sometimes recaptured.

R310.p: Places where fugitives or captives hide to escape their pursuers.

R311.r: Type 162*; *Fb “træ” III 865a; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 199a; BP I 429, II 195f.—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “arbres”; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 341 n. 230; S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 62; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 145, 346.
R311.p: A fugitive takes refuge by climbing into a tree to hide from pursuers.

R311.1.r: Dh II 40ff.; N. A. Indian: Kroeber JAFL XXI 225.
R311.1.p: Trees magically conceal a fugitive so that pursuers cannot find him.

R311.1.1.p: A fugitive is hidden by trees that magically conceal him, with a thorn thicket serving as the hiding place.

R311.2.p: A king escapes his pursuers by slipping into a hollow tree inside his own hall.

R311.3.p: A kidnapped child is discovered hidden inside a hollow tree.

R311.4.p: A tree stretches or grows to shelter a fugitive, hiding them from those chasing them.

R312.p: A fugitive escapes pursuers by fleeing into a forest, where it serves as a safe hiding place.

R312.1.p: Lovers who run away together to avoid their families find safety in a forest.

R313.p: A princess hides from pursuers by concealing herself in straw.

R314.p: A Black man takes refuge by hiding under a princess's throne.

R315.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo, (Greenland): Rasmussen I 150.
R315.p: A cave serves as a hiding place where a fugitive takes shelter.

R315.1.r: (Cf. R225, T35.) Schoepperle 391ff.; Irish myth: Cross.
R315.1.p: Lovers who elope hide from pursuit in a cave.

R315.2.p: Christians take refuge from non-Christians in a cave, where they are crushed to death.

R316.p: A fugitive takes refuge on a rock standing out in the sea.

R316.1.p: A fugitive escapes pursuers by reaching an island and staying there for safety.

R317.r: Fb “kilde” II 118b; Irish myth: Cross; Africa (Benga): Nassau 225 No. 33, (Kaffir): Theal 129, (Basuto): Jacottet 160 No. 23.
R317.p: A well or spring serves as a hiding place where a fugitive takes shelter.

R318.p: A girl hides from danger by concealing herself inside the skin of her dead mother.

R318.1.p: A boy hides under an animal skin so that he will not be seen and so that no prophecy about him will be fulfilled.

R321.r: (Cf. R324.) Greek: Fox 250; Hindu: Keith 76; Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 218 No. 98; Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 360; N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 291f. nn. 71, 71a; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 158, 164, (Jivaro): ibid. 149.
R321.p: Fugitives rise into the air and become stars, escaping their pursuers.

R321.1.p: A sister flees to the stars to avoid marrying her brother; he becomes thunder and she becomes lightning.

R321.2.p: A pursued hero escapes by going up to the moon.

R322.r: Scottish: Campbell-McKay 1 n., 25; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 95.
R322.p: A fugitive takes refuge in an eagle's nest, out of reach of pursuers.

R323.p: A fugitive escapes pursuit by fleeing up into the sky or heavens, where pursuers cannot follow.

R323.1.p: A murderer escapes his pursuers by climbing up to the sky on a rope that reaches the heavens.

R323.2.p: A murderer escapes his pursuers by flying up to the sky in a magic chariot.

R324.p: A fugitive supernaturally rises into the air to get away from danger.

R324.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 81, 86, (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 315, 541f., (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 151, (Greenland): Rasmussen III 99f., Rink 320, 455, 460.
R324.1.p: A character escapes from a battle by flying away through the air.

R325.r: Fb “kirke” II 125b; Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 276 n. 4; Jewish: *Neuman; Gaster Thespis 303f.; Japanese: Ikeda.
R325.p: A church or altar serves as a place of sanctuary where a pursued person is safe from capture.

R325.1.p: A devil chasing the ghost of a wicked man is stopped when the ghost pushes his head through a chapel window to find safety.

R325.2.p: In answer to prayer, an idol splits open to hide a fugitive, then closes again behind him.

R325.3.p: A saint offers a murderer protection and a place of refuge from those seeking to punish him.

R326.p: A fugitive escapes pursuit by getting away into fairyland.

R327.p: The earth opens up to swallow a pursued fugitive and keep him from his enemies.

R331.p: A hero seeks and receives protection by taking refuge at a king's court.

R335.r: West Indies: *Flowers 573 —75, Parsons MAFLS XVIII (3) 26 No. 6.
R335.p: Animals being chased find safety by getting up onto a roof.

R336.p: A pursued creature hides for safety under an overturned kettle or pot.

R341.p: A person escapes danger through a miraculous or divine intervention by Providence.

R341.1.p: Lightning strikes the branch a man is hanging from, and the delay gives him time to prove his innocence.

R345.p: Special cities are set aside as places where a person who has killed accidentally or is pursued may seek refuge.

R350.p: A fugitive who has escaped is found and captured again by his pursuers.

R351.r: *Type 408; *Cox 503; *Cosquin Contes indiens 85ff.; *Köhler-Bolte I 281; Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 64 to Gonzenbach No. 14; Malone PMLA XLIII 399.—India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 212, Dixon 140 n. 21, 226 n. 33; New Hebrides, Torres Straits, New Guinea: ibid. 140 n. 21; Melanesia: ibid. 226 n. 33; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 352 n. 270.
R351.p: A fugitive is discovered because his or her reflection shows in water, revealing the hiding place.

R351.1.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 156, 161.
R351.1.p: Milk drops from a woman's breast onto a tiger's leg, revealing where she is hiding up a tree.

R352.p: Lovers who flee from slavery are caught and taken back into bondage.

R355.p: A girl who runs off to marry her lover is caught and brought back by her parents.
